thread.title: Dow Drops 92 Points Because "Only a Fool" Believes the U.S. Can Withstand a Trade War

author: Barron's
title: Dow Drops 92 Points Because "Only a Fool" Believes the U.S. Can Withstand a Trade War
text:
Womp Womp . It's the trade war's market; we're just living in it. Another round of threats from the White House sank hopes that we're on the cusp of a tariff agreement, and took the stock market with it . In today's After the Bell , we…
Getty Images ABMD
A Case of the Mondays
Stocks slumped across the board Monday, after China threatened to pull out of talks with the U.S. if another round of tariffs goes into effect-and tech didn't help much.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 92.55 points, or 0.35%, to 26,062.12, while the S&P 500 slid 16.18 points, or 0.56%, to 2888.80 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 114.25 points, or 1.43%, to 7895.79.
It's easy to understand what has markets so spooked: Investors were thrilled to hear that the U.S. and China were coming back to the table for talks, so if negotiations are canceled, we'll be that much closer to staring down the barrel at a full-blown trade war, which no one wants.
Yes, the U.S. market has held up so far in the face of tariffs, unlike other markets, but "only a fool would believe that the U.S. economy can withstand a protracted trade war," says Eaton Vance's Lew Piantedosi. Our economy has remained resilient so far, but it's difficult to imagine that continuing, given how interconnected the world is and how large, multinational companies rely on global trade, if both countries go nuclear.
The administration surely knows this, and for a president who "hangs his hat on how well the market does," it would be extremely undesirable to spark a selloff, especially ahead of the midterms. That leads Piantedosi to be confident that today's setback aside, an armistice isn't out of the question.
A controlled descent is all the more desirable given that the market can't go up forever. While the U.S. "remains the pacesetter of the global economic expansion as growth weakens elsewhere," FTSE Russell's Alec Young writes, it's not invincible. "Global growth is downshifting," and most economists still expect gross domestic product to slow across most major regions next year, including the U.S. and China, "the two powerhouses behind nearly all global growth this past decade," Young continues.
Yikes. At least we still have tech right? Well, not so much today, as the Nasdaq's decline demonstrated. Amazon.com ( AMZN ) is embroiled in a suspected data leak including bribe-taking employees, and concerns about the new iPhone and suppliers dinged Apple ( AAPL ).
Well, Apple may have lost some shine, and while the FANGs- Facebook ( FB ), Amazon, Netflix ( NFLX ) and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL)-may be gunning for its perch as the world's most valuable company, none has "managed to create quite the same euphoria surrounding Apple in its prime," notes Leuthold's Kristen Perleberg. Like other giants of the S&P 500 before it, Apple will likely grizzle and fade, but fear not: A "new company [will] eventually ascertain this reputation (as history suggests it will)."
So FAANG, and maybe even tech in general, may eventually yield its crown as market leader, but another group will surely pick up its place and lead stocks higher. Who knows, maybe if we finally get a resolution on tariffs, it could be industrials , and CATBO-Caterpillar (CAT) and Boeing (BA) will ride again .
